claims.text: A manifest is a file, by convention YAML, declaring objects: apiVersion and kind give the type, metadata the name, and for objects such as a Pod, spec the desired state (Namespace has no spec; ConfigMap uses data).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Overview > Working with Objects > Objects In Kubernetes (Required fields; Object spec and status)

claims.text: Kubernetes objects are records of intent: once created, Kubernetes constantly works to ensure the object exists and its actual state (status) matches the desired state (spec).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Objects In Kubernetes (Object spec and status)

claims.text: kubectl apply -f <file> creates the objects declared in the file, or updates existing objects to match it (declarative object configuration).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Configuration Files; kubectl apply reference

claims.text: kubectl apply returns after the API server has accepted and stored the object; it does not wait for the Pod's containers to be running (hence kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready in the script).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: kubectl apply / kubectl wait reference; Pod lifecycle (Pending phase includes time downloading images)

claims.text: After the Pod is stored it is assigned to a worker node, which learns of it from the API server, pulls the image if not present (IfNotPresent default for non-latest tags) and starts the container; meanwhile STATUS shows Pending or ContainerCreating.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Pod Lifecycle (Pending, container states Waiting reason ContainerCreating)

claims.text: Applying an unchanged manifest again makes no change and kubectl prints '<kind>/<name> unchanged' (pod/web unchanged).
To change a live object declaratively you edit the manifest and run kubectl apply again; Kubernetes computes and makes the changes needed.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Configuration Files (How to update objects)

claims.text: Most fields of an existing Pod's spec are immutable; an apply changing one is rejected with an error ('pod updates may not change fields other than ...'), and the Pod must be deleted and applied again.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Pods (Pod update and replacement: most of the metadata/spec are immutable)

claims.text: scripts/k8s/apply-web-pod.sh@stage-2 lines 8-20: delete pod web --ignore-not-found, apply web-pod.yaml, kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web --timeout=120s, get pod web, apply again; output: created, condition met, 1/1 Running, unchanged.
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web blocks until the Pod's Ready condition is true or the timeout passes; Ready means the containers are ready to serve (shown as 1/1 READY, Running).
At stage-2 Đơn Hàng's manifests live in Git under deploy/k8s/ (namespace.yaml, api.yaml, db.yaml, redis.yaml, keycloak.yaml, mailpit.yaml, api-configmap.yaml, plus lessons/ and migrate/).
Opinion: keeping manifests in Git makes each change to the cluster a reviewed commit and lets the repository record what should run, when changes go through pull requests.
